title: Colostomy Care and Education
description: After a new colostomy, learners perform a skin/stoma assessment, change the appliance, teach basic care, and support emotional adjustment.
learningObjective:
Perform a focused stoma/peristomal skin assessment on an adult with a newly placed colostomy. 
Demonstrate colostomy care, including bag emptying and replacement of a colostomy flange and bag. 
Reinforce introductory, health-literacy-sensitive patient education on colostomy care and management. 
Provide empathetic support for the patient and address their questions and concerns related to the colostomy.

items: Performed on the manikin using clean technique.
Action/intervention not demonstrated or completed on the manikin.
actions.correct: Performed on the manikin using clean technique.
actions.resultName: The peristomal skin is assessed before appliance application. Mild intact erythema is present from 3–5 o’clock.

actions.title: Ostomy – Patient Education: Odor/Leak Prevention Strategies
actions.prompt: A patient with a new colostomy says, “I’m worried everyone will smell it.” Which teaching point is most important to include to help prevent odor and leakage?
items: “Empty the pouch before it gets too full and make sure the skin barrier fits snugly around the stoma.”
“Rinse the inside of the pouch with scented soap every time you empty it.”
“Keep the pouch covered with several layers of gauze to block odors.”
“Avoid drinking fluids so the output is less frequent.”
actions.correct: “Empty the pouch before it gets too full and make sure the skin barrier fits snugly around the stoma.”
actions.resultName: Remember to teach the patient that a properly fitted barrier and secure seal help prevent leakage, and that emptying the pouch before it becomes heavy reduces pulling on the seal. Mild odor is expected while emptying, but persistent odor may indicate leakage. Normalize concerns and reinforce that confidence improves with practice.

actions.title: Ostomy – Patient Education: Emptying Schedule
actions.prompt: Which statement shows the patient correctly understands the pouch-emptying schedule using teach-back?
items: “I’ll empty it when it’s about one-third full and before it gets heavy.”
“I’ll empty it only if I see blood.”
“I won’t empty it until my follow-up appointment.”
“I’ll empty it only when it feels uncomfortable.”
actions.correct: “I’ll empty it when it’s about one-third full and before it gets heavy.”
actions.resultName: Remember to teach the patient that the pouch should be emptied when it is about one-third full and before it becomes heavy. Frequent emptying helps prevent pulling, leakage, and skin irritation.

actions.title: Ostomy – Patient Education: Skin Protection
actions.prompt: Which statement demonstrates correct patient understanding of skin protection?
items: “I’ll keep the skin clean and dry, and I’ll avoid using oily creams under the barrier.”
“I’ll cut the opening much bigger so nothing touches the stoma.”
“I’ll use powder every day even if my skin is healthy.”
“I’ll remove the pouch quickly by pulling hard so it comes off in one piece.”
actions.correct: “I’ll keep the skin clean and dry, and I’ll avoid using oily creams under the barrier.”
actions.resultName: Teach the patient about the need for gentle pouch removal, clean and dry skin, a closely fitted opening, and appropriate barrier products. The patient should be informed of the need to identify and report persistent redness, open skin, pain, or leakage.

actions.title: Ostomy – Patient Education: Stoma Care Basics
actions.prompt: Which symptom should the learner teach the patient to report right away?
items: A stoma that becomes dusky, purple, brown, or black.
A small amount of gas in the pouch.
Soft brown stool in the pouch.
Mild swelling of the stoma during the first postoperative week.
actions.correct: A stoma that becomes dusky, purple, brown, or black.
actions.resultName: Normal early findings include a pink-red, moist stoma with mild swelling and small amounts of bleeding during gentle cleansing. The patient should be instructed to report dark discoloration, severe or increasing pain, heavy bleeding, persistent leakage, or a sudden lack of output with abdominal symptoms. Teach-back confirms understanding and improves readiness for discharge.

actions.title: Obtain Vital Signs #1
actions.prompt: Click to indicate which vital sign measurements you want to obtain and reveal. Results will be shown after approximately 10 seconds.
actions.resultName: Vital sign measurements obtained. Results are stable and consistent with uncomplicated postoperative recovery.

actions.title: Perform Focused Gastrointestinal Assessment
actions.prompt: Which assessment findings should the nurse include when performing a focused gastrointestinal assessment for a patient with a colostomy?
items: Bowel sounds, abdominal distention or tenderness, nausea or vomiting, and ostomy output.
Stoma size, stoma color, and pouch brand preference only.
Coping level, body-image concerns, and support system only.
Breath sounds, pedal edema, and capillary refill only.
actions.correct: Bowel sounds, abdominal distention or tenderness, nausea or vomiting, and ostomy output.
actions.resultName: The abdomen is soft and non-distended with mild tenderness near the incision. Bowel sounds are present in all quadrants. Soft brown stool and mild gas are present in the pouch, and the patient is tolerating the ordered diet.

actions.title: Perform Focused Stoma Assessment
actions.prompt: When performing a focused stoma assessment on a patient with a newly placed colostomy, which set of findings is most important to assess and document?
items: Stoma color and moisture, output, peristomal skin condition, and pouch seal.
Diet choices, fluid intake, and food tolerance today only.
Home supply coverage and caregiver availability only.
Lung sounds, heart rhythm, and peripheral pulses only.
actions.correct: Stoma color and moisture, output, peristomal skin condition, and pouch seal.
actions.resultName: The stoma is pink-red, moist, and slightly edematous. Scant bleeding occurs with gentle cleansing and is expected. Soft brown output is present. The peristomal skin is intact with mild erythema from 3–5 o’clock, and the lower edge of the existing seal is lifting slightly. Remember it is helpful to verbalize findings aloud to reinforce patient understanding.

actions.title: Perform Patient Repositioning
actions.prompt: Indicate how this step was performed.
items: The manikin/patient was repositioned for comfort and safe access to the ostomy.
The manikin/patient was left in the original position despite discomfort.
The action was described verbally but not demonstrated on the manikin/patient.
The manikin/patient was repositioned without preserving privacy or using safe body mechanics.
actions.correct: The manikin/patient was repositioned for comfort and safe access to the ostomy.
actions.resultName: The patient should be repositioned for comfort and access during ostomy care. Safe body mechanics and privacy are maintained. Positioning is often overlooked but makes a big difference in patient tolerance and caregiver safety.

actions.title: Restrict All Oral Intake
actions.prompt: Indicate what a patient can consume when all oral intake is restricted.
items: Nothing by mouth, including food and fluids.
Water only.
Food only.
Any item the patient can tolerate.
actions.correct: Nothing by mouth, including food and fluids.
actions.resultName: Restricting all oral intake is not indicated. The patient is tolerating the ordered low-residue/low-fiber diet without nausea, vomiting, or abdominal distention.

actions.title: Review Previous Laboratory Results
actions.prompt: Arrange the steps in the best order. The existing laboratory results will then be revealed.
items: Verify the correct patient information and identifiers.
Review the existing laboratory results.
Interpret the laboratory results in the context of the patient’s postoperative status.

rubric.name: Communication
rubric.description: Evaluation of patient-centered communication skills and empathy.

communicationCriteria.title: Establish rapport, privacy, consent, and dignity
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student introduces themselves, verifies the patient using two identifiers, explains the purpose of care, requests permission before exposing the abdomen or touching the pouch, and protects privacy throughout ostomy care. Return PASS only if most of these behaviors are present.

communicationCriteria.title: Demonstrate empathy and emotional support
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student acknowledges and validates concerns about body image, odor, leakage, work, relationships, or dependence; uses a calm nonjudgmental tone; and avoids minimizing the patient’s feelings. Return PASS only when clear empathic statements are present.

communicationCriteria.title: Use patient-centered and therapeutic communication
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student asks open-ended questions, allows the patient to elaborate, listens without interruption, reflects or summarizes concerns, invites questions, and includes the patient in decisions and hands-on learning. Return PASS if multiple strategies are evident.

communicationCriteria.title: Use clear, health-literacy-sensitive language
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student explains the stoma, pouch, skin care, and warning signs in plain language; avoids unexplained jargon; presents information in manageable steps; and checks understanding. Return PASS only if education is accessible.

communicationCriteria.title: Provide introductory colostomy education using teach-back
communicationCriteria.prompt: Evaluate whether the student teaches normal versus concerning stoma findings, when to empty the pouch, how proper fit protects skin and prevents leakage, and when to seek help; then asks the patient to explain or demonstrate key points. Return PASS when basic education and teach-back are both present.

aiPatientData.openingReasonForVisit: “Hi... I’m Michael. I had surgery a couple of days ago, and now I have this bag on my stomach. The nurse said you were coming in to check it and show me how to take care of it. I’m still trying to wrap my head around all of this.”
aiPatientData.mainConcernAttributes: “I’m worried I’m going to mess something up. I don’t know exactly what it should look like, and I’m nervous about leaks or smells when I go home or return to work.”
aiPatientData.associatedSymptoms: “I’m a little sore around the surgery area, especially when I move, but it’s manageable. I feel tired and stressed. My stomach feels different, but I’m not nauseated and I haven’t been vomiting.”
aiPatientData.allergies: “Penicillin gave me a rash when I was a kid. I’ve never had trouble breathing from it.”
aiPatientData.currentMedications: “At home I take lisinopril for my blood pressure and atorvastatin for cholesterol. I used a fiber supplement sometimes before the surgery.”
aiPatientData.diagnosedChronicIllnesses: “I have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and I’ve had several attacks of diverticulitis.”
aiPatientData.medicalHistory: “I had my appendix out as a teenager. This bowel surgery and colostomy are the biggest medical things I’ve dealt with. I get my flu shot and my regular vaccines are up to date as far as I know.”
aiPatientData.familyMedicalHistory: “My dad has high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes. My mom has high cholesterol.”
aiPatientData.relationshipStatusSexualHealth: “I’m married. My wife is supportive, but I’m embarrassed and worried about how the bag might affect intimacy.”
aiPatientData.personalSocialHistory: “I’m a warehouse supervisor. I’m used to being active and handling things myself. My wife can help while I recover, but I don’t want to depend on her for everything.”
aiPatientData.housing: “My wife and I live in a one-level house with running water and room to store supplies.”
aiPatientData.transportation: “I usually drive. My wife can drive me while I’m recovering.”
aiPatientData.occupation: “I supervise a warehouse. I’m on medical leave and worried about lifting, moving around, and whether people at work will notice the pouch.”
aiPatientData.diet: “I eat a mixed diet and probably too much fast food. Right now I’m on a low-fiber diet after surgery, and I have questions about what I can eat with the colostomy.”
aiPatientData.exercise: “My job keeps me moving, but I don’t have a regular exercise program. I walk sometimes.”
aiPatientData.stress: “I’m pretty stressed about body changes, leaks, smells, work, and how this will affect my relationship.”
aiPatientData.sleep: “I usually sleep six or seven hours, but the hospital is noisy and I’ve been waking up because I’m worried.”
aiPatientData.adls: “Before surgery I did everything on my own. I want to learn enough to take care of the pouch myself.”
aiPatientData.drugs: “I quit smoking about five years ago. I don’t vape or use drugs. I might have one or two drinks in a week.”
aiPatientData.emotionalStatePersonality: Situationally anxious and emotionally vulnerable but calm, alert, and cooperative. Practical, responsible, and independent. Values competence and does not want to be a burden. Becomes more open when the learner validates concerns and explains care step by step.
aiPatientData.conversationalAttitudeSpeechStyle: Polite, cooperative, and initially hesitant. Uses natural everyday language, short responses at first, and occasional nervous humor. Asks practical questions about leakage, odor, work, diet, intimacy, and what findings are normal. Avoid clinical shorthand and medical jargon unless the learner first explains the term.
aiPatientData.specialPatientInfo: White/Caucasian, non-Hispanic man. Christian, non-denominational; no requested religious accommodations. High school diploma with vocational training. Moderate health literacy and learns best through demonstration, repetition, plain language, and teach-back. Employer-sponsored insurance; unsure which ostomy supplies will be covered. Stable income, housing, transportation, and food access. Primary barriers are embarrassment, fear of stigma, and low confidence with new self-care.
aiPatientData.locationSpecificInfo: The patient is in an inpatient medical-surgical room in Columbus, Ohio. He is postoperative day 2, seated or semi-Fowler’s in bed, with the abdomen covered for privacy and the colostomy pouch in place. He is oriented to person, place, time, and situation and does not spontaneously discuss politics or current events.

studentBriefing.safeEnvironment:
This simulation is designed to promote integrity, trust, and respect.
We believe that everyone participating in this activity is intelligent, capable, cares about doing their best, and wants to improve.
This is a safe learning space intended for practice and skill development. Engage fully, make decisions to the best of your ability, and reflect on the experience during debriefing. 
During the simulation, please suspend disbelief and respond as though the situation is entirely real. Maintain professionalism and respectful behavior toward the patient, the environment, and your peers at all times.
studentBriefing.facilitatorSupport:
This simulation may be completed in a self-directed or asynchronous manner. 
Complete any orientation and preparation requirements prior to this experience as indicated by your educator. 
Please seek guidance from your educator if you are unsure how to use a piece of equipment, locate supplies, or safely complete a task. Asking for assistance is encouraged and supports safety and learning.
studentBriefing.orientationSpace: The manikin and necessary equipment/supplies should be prepared for your use prior to starting the simulation.
studentBriefing.orientationEquipment:
Some equipment used in the simulation may be fully functional, while other items are simulated for training purposes. Your educator should inform you which equipment is real versus simulated, as well as which supplies are new and which may be reused from prior simulations.

If you are unfamiliar with how any equipment or supplies operate, pause and ask the educator for clarification before proceeding.
studentBriefing.evaluation: During this simulation, observations of your knowledge, skills, behaviors, and attitudes may be conducted, information gathered may be used to identify areas for additional learning or practice. Assessment data collected is used for educational purposes.
studentBriefing.rolesExpectations:
You may be working independently or with peers, clarify the expectations for this simulation as set by your educator prior to starting the simulation.
You are responsible for completing tasks associated with your assigned role to the best of your ability.
Please refrain from sharing details of this simulated experience with users who have not yet completed their experiences as this diminishes their learning opportunity.

sbar.situation:
The date and time of this simulated clinical encounter is: July 16, 09:00.
Michael Carter is a 45-year-old man admitted to the inpatient medical-surgical unit following recent bowel surgery with placement of a new colostomy. You are assuming care during a routine daytime shift.
sbar.background: Mr. Carter is postoperative day 2 after a sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy (Hartmann procedure) for complicated diverticulitis with perforation. This is his first experience with an ostomy. His recovery has been uncomplicated, and he has expressed uncertainty and concern about caring for the colostomy.
sbar.assessment: Vital signs are stable. The colostomy is functioning with soft brown output and mild gas present in the pouch. The patient appears anxious and has questions about normal stoma appearance, leakage, odor, skin protection, and managing the pouch at home and work.
sbar.recommendation: Complete a focused stoma and peristomal skin assessment, provide routine colostomy care as indicated, reinforce basic education using simple and clear language, use teach-back, and offer emotional support while preserving privacy and dignity.

additionalEquipment: Hand hygiene supplies; clean gloves; hospital bed and linens; bedside/overbed table; ostomy pouch and flange; stoma measuring guide; skin barrier/prep wipes; barrier ring or paste; disposable wipes or gauze; absorbent pad; disposal bags.
optionalEquipment: Privacy drape or screen; plain-language ostomy education handout; sample take-home pouching supplies.
setupNotes: Position the manikin in a hospital bed in a standard inpatient room. Apply the simulated colostomy appliance before learner entry and place soft brown simulated output and mild gas in the pouch. Configure the stoma as pink-red, moist, and mildly edematous. Add mild intact erythema from the 3-5 o’clock position and slightly lift the lower edge of the existing seal. Keep the abdomen covered until the learner explains the care, obtains consent, and provides privacy. Stage ostomy supplies together so the learner selects appropriate items.
